lead: A soldered board can fail even when every chip is good: a joint is open, a net is shorted, or a pin is not connected. Boundary scan and in-circuit testing find these faults after assembly. Boundary scan uses a small test port and a chain of cells at each pin, defined by IEEE 1149.1, often called JTAG. In-circuit test uses physical probes on test points. Both are board-level tests, used in factories and repair benches before software is allowed to trust the hardware.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.2 for debug interfaces and Unit 3 for digital I/O.

blocks.text: Testing a bare chip is not enough. After reflow, a board can have an open joint, a solder bridge between two nets, a missing resistor, a bent pin, or a part placed the wrong way. A net is one copper connection that should join a set of pins. A test point is a small pad or via that a probe can touch. These faults are mechanical and chemical, not software bugs. Board-level tests look for them before firmware runs. The two common methods are boundary scan, which uses logic inside chips, and in-circuit test (ICT), which uses physical probes. Both answer a simple question: are the pins joined as the schematic says? This check belongs to the integration and testing stage of the EDLC.

sections.h3: JTAG boundary scan: TAP, registers and instructions

blocks.text: IEEE 1149.1 adds a test access port (TAP) to a chip. The TAP uses five signals. TCK is the test clock. TMS is the test mode select, sampled on TCK to move a small state machine. TDI is test data in and TDO is test data out. TRST is an optional test reset; when absent, a TMS sequence resets the TAP. The TAP controller is the state machine. It loads an instruction into the instruction register (IR). The instruction connects a chosen data register between TDI and TDO. Two data registers matter here. The boundary-scan register (BSR) has one cell for each device pin. A cell can capture the pin value, or drive the pin. Cells of all chips on a board are wired as one long shift register, the scan chain. A test vector is a bit pattern shifted through the chain; the captured bits are shifted out and compared with the expected pattern.

blocks.where: t<sub>shift</sub> is the time to shift one vector in seconds; N<sub>bits</sub> is the total number of boundary-scan cells in the chain; f<sub>TCK</sub> is the TCK frequency in hertz.

blocks.text: Common instructions are: BYPASS, which puts one bypass cell in the chain so other devices can be reached quickly; IDCODE, which reads the device identity; SAMPLE, which captures pin values during normal operation without driving them; and EXTEST, which drives pins from the BSR to test board nets. Only a few syllabi teach the full 16-state TAP machine. For exams, know that TCK and TMS move through states such as Capture-DR, Shift-DR and Update-DR.

sections.h3: In-circuit test, flying probe and design for test

blocks.text: In-circuit test (ICT) checks an assembled board with physical probes. A bed-of-nails fixture has spring-loaded pins, one per test point, pressed on the board at once. A flying probe machine moves one or two probes to each test point in turn; it needs no custom fixture but is slower. ICT can measure resistance, capacitance, shorts and opens, and can power a small part of the board. It can also program flash or run a simple functional check.

Design for test (DFT) makes these checks possible: keep test points accessible, avoid hidden nets under parts, add boundary-scan chains, and provide a way to isolate buses. Coverage is the fraction of the intended faults that a test can detect. High coverage does not mean zero escapes. Built-in self-test (BIST) puts pattern generators and checkers inside a chip. It can test memory and logic at speed, but BIST does not see a cracked solder joint; boundary scan and ICT do that.

examples.question: A board has a scan chain of 4 devices. Each device has 32 boundary-scan cells. TCK runs at 1 MHz. Ignore capture and update overhead. (a) How many bits are in one test vector? (b) How long does one vector take to shift in? (c) For 1000 vectors, what is the total shift test time?
steps: Total cells = 4 × 32 = 128 cells. One cell holds one bit in the scan path, so one vector = 128 bits.
TCK = 1 MHz = 1,000,000 clocks per second. One bit per clock, so shift time = 128 ÷ 1,000,000 s = 0.000128 s = 128 µs.
For 1000 vectors, total shift time = 1000 × 128 µs = 128,000 µs = 128 ms.
examples.answer: One vector has 128 bits, takes 128 µs to shift, and 1000 vectors take 128 ms of shift time.
examples.check:
bits = 4 * 32
f_tck = 1_000_000
shift_s = bits / f_tck
shift_us = shift_s * 1_000_000
test_us = 1000 * shift_us
test_ms = test_us / 1000
print(int(bits))
print(int(shift_us))
print(int(test_ms))

traps: Boundary scan is not a full-speed functional test. EXTEST checks interconnect and pin drive; it does not prove the chip core works at full application speed.
TDI is data into the chain, TDO is data out. Reversing them flips the shift direction in an answer.
BYPASS shortens the chain; EXTEST drives pins. They are not the same instruction.
ICT with bed-of-nails needs physical test points; BIST runs inside the chip and cannot detect every solder open.
Coverage is not yield: coverage is fault detection, yield is good boards per batch.

quiz.q: Name the four mandatory TAP signals in IEEE 1149.1 and state the job of each.
quiz.a: TCK is the test clock, TMS selects the state machine path, TDI is test data in, TDO is test data out. TRST is optional.

quiz.q: Why does the BYPASS instruction exist?
quiz.a: BYPASS shortens the scan chain through a device that is not being tested. Fewer clocks are needed to shift a vector to the devices that matter.

quiz.q: A chain has 6 devices with 16 boundary-scan cells each. TCK is 2 MHz. Find the vector length and the one-vector shift time.
quiz.a: Cells = 6 × 16 = 96, so vector = 96 bits. Shift time = 96 ÷ 2,000,000 s = 48 µs.

quiz.q: A board passes EXTEST but fails at speed in the application. Does this contradict boundary scan? Explain.
quiz.a: No. EXTEST tests board nets and pin drive, often at low speed. It does not test core logic timing or software behaviour inside the chip.
A test fixture with many spring-loaded probes that touch the board's test points at the same time.
ICT uses external probes on an assembled board. BIST uses built-in pattern generators and checkers inside a chip. BIST cannot see a cracked solder joint.

quiz.q: Why can high fault coverage still allow faulty boards to ship? Give two reasons.
quiz.a: The fault model may miss real defects, such as intermittent joints or wrong part values. Coverage may be less than 100 percent, and test thresholds can pass marginal boards.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry adds IEEE 1149.6 for AC-coupled links, IEEE 1687 (IJTAG) for on-chip instruments, and chiplet test using boundary-scan-like access. EDA tools insert scan and BIST during synthesis, and factory test programs combine ICT, boundary scan and functional test.
